entry.title: Rewinding the Exponential: How We Keep Hardware Usage Down (12 minute read)
entry.content:
Cloudflare's data pipeline handles roughly two billion events per second while hardware capacity grows more slowly than traffic. Product-specific schemas, zstd compression, later replication, earlier sampling, and aggregation have collectively deferred the equivalent of two and a half years of hardware expansion.

entry.title: Redesigning Source Control at Anthropic (14 minute read)
entry.content:
Anthropic replaced Git with Scion after daily merges grew from roughly 2,500 to more than 30,000. The centralized system uses server-side commits, sparse checkouts, and layered caches, reducing its source control infrastructure's CPU and memory footprint by 200 times and freeing 25% of CI CPU capacity.

entry.title: A Year of Fast Apply: The Path to 10k Tokens per Second (13 minute read)
entry.content:
Relace explains how it built a small model that applies code edits at a reported 10,000 tokens per second using high-quality merge data, LoRA fine-tuning, FP8 quantization, and speculative decoding. Its training pipeline filtered 200,000 candidate examples down to about 145,000, using a judge calibrated against 500 manually reviewed merges. Relace Apply 3 supports a 256,000-token context and multiple diff formats, although improving frontier-model edit accuracy could eventually reduce the need for specialized apply models.

entry.title: How I Found a $90,000 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google (4 minute read)
entry.content:
Google's DevSite stored an OAuth secret inside a readable Flask session cookie and reused it as the cookie's signing key, allowing forged sessions to reach unsafe pickle deserialization. Timing-based tests confirmed unauthenticated code execution across the shared platform, earning a $90,000 bounty. The fix separates signing keys from OAuth credentials and removes sensitive serialized objects from client-controlled sessions.

entry.title: Can we Make React Faster using the React Compiler? (20 minute read)
entry.content:
React Compiler uses cache slots and tracks values that change together to avoid unnecessary work. In a 2,000-row microbenchmark, inlining alone slowed rendering from 444 ms to 1,038 ms by removing per-row caches, while adding block DOM updates cut it to 164 ms. These prototypes illustrate optimization opportunities, with workload and memory tradeoffs still to evaluate.

In production, fewer than 2% of submissions are rejected as stale, with median submit latency below 1.7 seconds.

entry.title: Human PR Review Is Next (12 minute read)
entry.content:

Independent review models, predefined guardrails, and automated review-and-fix cycles form the proposed safety net. A trading-bot rounding bug illustrates the tradeoff: fast fixes do not erase losses or compensate for gaps in the specification.

entry.title: The Dirty Pages Surprise: When a Read-Only Query Writes Terabytes (10 minute read)
entry.content:
A MonetDB count-distinct query saturates an NVMe drive with writes because Linux flushes dirty pages from temporary memory-mapped scratch files. Moving the scratch files to tmpfs cuts runtime from 73 minutes to 97 seconds, while workload-specific writeback tuning reaches about 100 seconds without moving them off disk.

entry.title: Jev and the Return of the Classifiers (11 minute read)
entry.content:
Jev returns typed choices, scores, or yes-or-no probabilities instead of generating prose, making bounded decisions fast and inexpensive. Its “zero hallucination” claim means outputs always fit the supplied schema, not that every decision is correct. The more important promise is calibrated confidence that can route uncertain cases to humans or slower reasoning models, though that calibration requires validation on real workloads.
